summary: RELOAD is a peer-to-peer signaling protocol that gives clients an abstract storage and messaging service across an overlay network of cooperating peers. It was designed to support peer-to-peer SIP (P2PSIP) but other applications can use it by defining new usages that specify what kinds of data to store.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers form a club where they all share storage and pass messages without a boss. RELOAD is the rulebook for the club.

questions: what is a node-id in reload
subtitle: A peer-to-peer overlay that lets cooperating nodes route messages and share small signed records without a central server.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer applications such as P2P SIP need to find each other and store small pieces of data across many machines that do not trust one another, most of them behind NATs or firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: RELOAD arranges nodes into an overlay network, routes each message hop by hop using Destination Lists and Via Lists, and stores signed data at the peers responsible for a Resource-ID. Certificates from an enrollment service identify every node, and ICE sets up connections across NATs.
tldr.outcome: Applications reuse the same overlay by defining a usage with new data Kinds, and a Chord-based algorithm is the mandatory-to-implement default. RFC 6940 is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting RFC listed.

facts.label: End-to-end retransmissions
facts.value: Up to 4, for 5 messages in total

today: RFC 6940 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the base protocol only; the SIP usage is described separately in a document the RFC refers to as [SIP-RELOAD].

sections.title: What RELOAD Provides
sections.content:
RFC 6940 defines RELOAD (REsource LOcation And Discovery), a peer-to-peer signaling protocol. A RELOAD Overlay Instance is a set of nodes arranged in a partly connected graph. Each node has a numeric Node-ID, and the overlay lets any node reach any other node within a small number of hops. It is also a small-scale storage network: records are stored under numeric addresses called Resource-IDs, and each peer is responsible for the data whose addresses fall in its share of the space.

The RFC lists the properties it was designed around: a security framework based on a central enrollment server, a usage model so new applications can define their own data types, NAT traversal built into the base protocol, a lightweight forwarding header, pluggable overlay algorithms, and support for clients. These were designed to meet the needs of P2P SIP, but RELOAD is not limited to SIP.

Not every node does the same work. Peers route messages and store data for others. Clients have a Node-ID and use the overlay to find resources and store their own data, but they do not route or store for anyone else. The RFC's example overlay has Node 85 as a client attached through Node 80, while Node 90 stays responsible for addresses 81 to 90.
sections.plainLanguage: RELOAD is the rulebook for a club of computers. Some members help carry messages and keep notes safe; others just use the club without helping out.

sections.title: The Layered Architecture
sections.content:
RELOAD is built from layers, each with one job. The Usage Layer holds application usages, such as a SIP usage, that define which data Kinds to store and how to secure them. Below the messaging service boundary sit the Message Transport component, which handles end-to-end request and response transactions, and the Storage component, which processes Store and Fetch requests.

The Topology Plug-in implements the chosen overlay algorithm and owns the Routing Table. The Forwarding and Link Management Layer moves a message to the next peer the plug-in picks and sets up connections through NATs using ICE. At the bottom, the Overlay Link Layer carries traffic directly between neighbors; this document defines TLS and DTLS for that role.

Reliability is split on purpose. Message Transport retransmits on a timer for end-to-end reliability but provides no congestion control, because RELOAD transactions use no more than two request-response pairs. Congestion control and per-hop retransmission live in the Forwarding and Link Management Layer.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a postal system with separate jobs: one person writes the letter, one decides the next stop, and one drives the truck between towns.

sections.title: How Messages Are Routed
sections.content:
RELOAD routes by Destination List, an ordered list of Node-IDs and, at the end, optionally a Resource-ID that works as a loose source route. To let the response find its way back, each message also carries a Via List that every forwarding node extends. The responder reverses the Via List to form the Destination List of the response. This default is called symmetric recursive routing, and all implementations MUST implement it.

A peer may instead keep per-transaction state and shorten the Via List. It can replace several entries with an opaque ID that only it can decode, which the RFC calls list compression. Peers may mix both styles even within one message. RELOAD also supports a basic iterative mode through the RouteQuery method, where a peer answers with the next hop instead of forwarding. Only the initiating node selects that mode.

Addressing matters. To reach the peer that controls a region of the space, a sender addresses a Resource-ID, not a Node-ID. A Resource-ID must be the only entry on a Destination List, and a message whose first entry is the wildcard Node-ID (all ones) is consumed by whoever receives it and never forwarded.

For reliability, an originator sets a timer to the overlay-reliability-timer and retransmits with the same transaction ID up to 4 times, for a total of 5 messages. Receivers MUST give semantically equivalent responses to retransmissions of the same request within the maximum request lifetime of 15 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person who passes your note writes their name on it, so the answer can walk back the same way through the same people.

sections.title: The RELOAD Message Format
sections.content:
Every message has three parts: a Forwarding Header, the Message Contents and a Security Block. Intermediate peers need to look only at the forwarding header. Integers use network byte order, and structures are written in a C-like presentation language based on the one used to define TLS.

The header starts with relo_token, which MUST be 0xd2454c4f (the string RELO with the high bit of the first byte set). Next come the overlay field (the lower 32 bits of the SHA-1 hash of the overlay name), a configuration sequence number, a version field (this document is version 1.0, value 0x0a) and a ttl that starts at 100 and is decremented at every hop. A 64-bit random transaction_id ties responses to requests and is also used for fragment reassembly. The Via List, Destination List and options follow.

In the contents, message_code values 0x1 to 0x7FFF come in pairs: requests are odd and the response is the request code plus 1. Code 0xFFFF means an error, and the body is an ErrorResponse with an error code and optional text. Defined errors include Error_Forbidden, Error_Not_Found, Error_TTL_Exceeded and Error_Config_Too_Old.

All messages MUST be signed by their originator. The Security Block carries the certificates needed to verify signatures plus the signature itself, and all implementations MUST support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures with SHA-256. The destination verifies the signature after reassembly; intermediate nodes do not.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is an envelope with a delivery label on the outside, the letter inside, and a signature on the back so you know who sent it.

sections.title: Connecting and Maintaining the Overlay
sections.content:
Because many nodes sit behind NATs, direct connections are made with the Attach method. Peer A gathers ICE candidates, puts them in an Attach request, and sends it through the overlay to B. B gathers its own candidates and answers, and then both run ICE connectivity checks. RELOAD implementations MUST implement full ICE. When two peers send Attach to each other at once, the one with the smaller Node-ID cancels its own request and answers the other, while the one with the larger Node-ID returns Error_In_Progress.

Attach does not change anyone's Routing Table. That is the job of Update, so a node that has only attached MUST NOT route messages through that connection to other peers. This keeps half-open states away: a client can simply Attach, while a peer also performs Join and Update.

The other methods in this layer are small. AppAttach opens a separate direct connection for an application protocol, identified by a 16-bit Application-ID. Ping tests connectivity and may carry up to 65535 bytes of padding to help find maximum packet sizes. ConfigUpdate pushes a new Configuration Document or new Kind definitions, and it is processed only if the sequence number is greater and the signature is valid.

Topology plug-ins use Join, Leave, Update, RouteQuery and Probe. The contents of Join, Leave and Update are defined by the overlay algorithm. Probe asks a node for the fraction of the overlay it covers (in parts per billion), the number of resources it stores, or its uptime in seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two kids can talk directly, they pass a note through friends saying where each can be reached. Once they agree on a meeting spot, they chat face to face.

sections.title: Links, Framing and Fragmentation
sections.content:
RELOAD currently defines three overlay link protocols: DTLS over UDP with Simple Reliability, TLS over TCP with a Framing Header and no ICE, and DTLS over UDP with Simple Reliability and no ICE. Any link protocol must authenticate the endpoint, protect traffic origin and integrity (including replay detection), and keep traffic confidential. New ones MUST be defined by Standards Action.

Each hop wraps a message in a very simple FramedMessage that carries a sequence number for data and an acknowledgement type. An ACK carries a 32-bit received bitmask covering the 32 most recent sequence numbers, which lets the sender estimate loss and round-trip time. Simple Reliability puts all the complexity on the sender: every message is ACKed and reliably retransmitted hop by hop. The sample stop-and-wait sender uses a default retransmission timeout of 500 ms, doubles the wait after each retransmission, gives new sequence numbers to retransmissions, and stops after 5 requests.

A message that is too big for a datagram link can be fragmented by any node on the path, but only the final destination reassembles it. Each fragment carries a full copy of the Via List, Destination List and options and at least 256 bytes of body. Receivers SHOULD discard incomplete fragments after the 15-second maximum request lifetime. An unfragmented message is encoded as a single last fragment at offset 0, giving a fragment field of 0xC0000000.
sections.plainLanguage: Each leg of the trip has its own mail carrier who gets a receipt for every parcel. Big parcels may be split into smaller boxes along the way, and only the last stop puts them back together.

sections.title: Storing and Fetching Data
sections.content:
Each Resource-ID is one location in the overlay, and a location can hold values of several Kinds, each identified by a 32-bit Kind-ID. A Kind defines what is stored, its data model and its access control. Three data models are defined: a single value (a new value overwrites the old), an array addressed by a zero-based numeric index, and a dictionary addressed by a key.

Every stored value is a StoredData with a storage_time in milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, a lifetime in seconds and a signature by the writer. A store with an older storage time than the existing value gets Error_Data_Too_Old, which blocks rollback attacks. A generation_counter works much like an HTTP ETag. A multi-Kind Store is atomic: if any part fails, everything is rolled back.

Four access control policies are defined. USER-MATCH allows a write only if the signer's user name hashes to the Resource-ID. NODE-MATCH does the same for a Node-ID. USER-NODE-MATCH works only with dictionaries and also requires the dictionary key to equal the signer's Node-ID. NODE-MULTIPLE accepts a Node-ID hashed with a small integer.

The methods are Store, Fetch, Stat (metadata without the data) and Find (the closest Resource-ID of a Kind known to a peer). There is no Remove: an owner stores a value with exists set to false, ideally with a lifetime at least as long as the value it replaces. Two usages are defined here: a Certificate Store, where nodes store their certificates, and a TURN Server Usage for finding relay servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The overlay is a giant set of lockers. Only the owner has the key to put a note in their locker, every note is signed, and nobody can swap in an older note without being caught.

sections.title: The Chord Overlay Algorithm
sections.content:
RELOAD itself does not fix a topology, but it defines one algorithm that every implementation MUST support: CHORD-RELOAD, an adaptation of the Chord distributed hash table. Nodes sit on a ring, with all arithmetic modulo 2 to the power of the Node-ID length. Each peer keeps a Neighbor Table with at least three peers on each side and a Finger Table whose first entry is the peer halfway around the ring, the second a quarter, and so on. The neighbors keep the ring correct, while the fingers give lookups in O(log N) time.

A peer is responsible for a Resource-ID k if k is less than or equal to its own Node-ID and greater than the Node-ID of the previous peer. Resource-IDs are 128 bits: the hash is SHA-1 truncated to its most significant 128 bits. To route, a peer forwards to the entry in its Routing Table with the largest Node-ID in the interval between itself and k.

For redundancy, a responsible peer stores the data, then sends Store requests to its successor and to that peer's successor, marked as replicas. This protects against peer failure but not against malicious peers.

Joining follows nine steps: the joining node (JN) connects to a bootstrap node, attaches to the Admitting Peer (AP) for Resource-ID n+1, attaches to its neighbors and fingers, sends Join to AP, receives Stores of the data it will be responsible for, and then exchanges Updates. A JN MUST NOT send an Update placing itself in the overlay until it has attached to every peer that belongs in its Neighbor Table.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone stands in a big circle and knows a few people next to them and a few people far across. To find someone, you pass the message to whoever you know who is closest to them.

sections.title: Enrollment and Bootstrap
sections.content:
A new node starts with just an overlay name. It looks up a configuration server with a DNS SRV query for the service name reload-config, then fetches a Configuration Document over HTTPS from a well-known path, for example https://example.com/.well-known/reload-config for the overlay name example.com. This XML document (content type application/p2p-overlay+xml) carries trust anchors, enrollment servers, bootstrap nodes and parameters, so it must be obtained securely.

Defaults include a bootstrap port of 6084, a maximum message size of 5000 bytes, an initial TTL of 100 and an overlay reliability timer of 3000 ms. The Node-ID length is between 16 and 20 bytes, with 16 as the default.

If the document lists an enrollment server, credentials are required. The node sends an HTTPS POST with a PKCS#10 certificate request, plus a username and password if needed, and gets back a certificate whose subjectAltName holds cryptographically random Node-IDs and one user name. The server SHOULD return the same Node-IDs when the same user comes back, so data does not have to be re-stored. If the overlay permits self-signed certificates, the Node-ID is a digest of the public key.

To join, the node connects to a bootstrap node over DTLS or TLS and sends an Attach whose destination is its own Node-ID plus 1. After joining, it may cache directly connected peers as future bootstrap nodes; the suggested number is 10.
sections.plainLanguage: To join the club you first look up its address, pick up the rulebook, show some ID to get a membership card, and then knock on the door of a member who is always home.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RELOAD protects communication at three levels: connections are secured with TLS or DTLS, each message is signed, and each stored object is signed by its creator. The enrollment server's ability to stop attackers from getting many certificates is described as one of the cornerstones of the design. All implementations MUST implement certificate-based security.

Signed storage means a peer can refuse to store or return a value, but it cannot forge data owned by someone else. Per-Kind maximum sizes, defined in the configuration, create a distributed quota. Monotonically increasing storage times defend against rollback. The RFC says parallel searches over replicated registrations are the way to counter peers that withhold data.

Against routing attacks, random Node-IDs from the enrollment server limit Sybil attacks and make Eclipse attacks harder, though not impossible. The initial TTL should be set slightly larger than the longest expected path to limit amplification from source routing, and implementations SHOULD discard messages whose Destination List contains duplicate entries.

An optional shared-secret mode uses TLS-PSK or TLS-SRP so that only holders of the key can form connections; it is meant for small groups. Passwords used as keys with TLS-PSK are open to dictionary attacks, so TLS-SRP is the better choice there. Self-signed certificates reduce security considerably and fit only closed networks of mutually trusting users.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is signed, like a notebook where each entry has the writer's own stamp. A mean member can throw notes away, but cannot make a fake note with someone else's stamp.
